_meta.source: Canonical bounded Evidence topics and completed primary-study summaries
_meta.license: Synthetic educational reference content for qualified review. No warranty.
_meta.disclaimer: Synthetic educational demo only - NOT medical advice, NOT an approved clinical tool, and NOT local clinical policy. Do not enter, transmit, or infer PHI or real encounter details. Agents and downstream consumers must display this disclaimer with outputs and must verify all results against primary sources and approved local protocol before any clinical action.
_meta.scope: Source-bound reference cards, not treatment gates or recruitment records. checkedAt records source access and scope checks, not full clinical certification; preserve each source access note and each card limitation.

topics.title: Acute ischemic stroke: reperfusion review
topics.summary: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline expands reperfusion evaluation, including selected large-core and basilar occlusions. Disability matters beyond the NIHSS total. Late or unknown-onset thrombolysis requires appropriate imaging selection; use the ischemic protocol for the full eligibility review.
consider: Is the deficit disabling despite a low NIHSS score?
Are onset certainty, vascular imaging and any required tissue imaging established?
Does the occlusion and imaging profile warrant prompt review by an EVT-capable team?
topics.caution: Expanded eligibility does not establish treatment clearance. A numeric NIHSS alone cannot resolve whether a deficit is disabling.

sources.title: AHA/ASA 2026 acute ischemic stroke guideline — official summary
sources.access: Official summary read; full guideline recommendations and eligibility tables were not reviewed for this card.

topics.title: TIA: evaluation and disposition
topics.summary: Resolved symptoms still require prompt evaluation. The AHA statement prioritizes diagnostic certainty, brain and vascular imaging, cardiac evaluation and a reliable prevention and follow-up plan. MRI with DWI is preferred for detecting tissue injury; CT with CTA can address hemorrhage and relevant arterial disease when appropriate.
consider: Does the history fit focal ischemia, and what competing diagnosis remains?
Have brain imaging, vascular imaging and relevant cardiac testing been completed or explicitly arranged?
Who owns outstanding results, prevention treatment and rapid neurology follow-up?
topics.caution: A risk score complements the evaluation; it does not establish the diagnosis or independently justify discharge. Recurrent or persistent deficits require acute stroke reassessment.

sources.title: AHA 2023 TIA diagnosis, workup and risk reduction statement — official summary
sources.access: Official summary read; full statement and disposition tables were not reviewed for this card.

topics.title: Spontaneous ICH: immediate priorities
topics.summary: Early ICH care combines assessment for expansion, smooth blood-pressure control, prompt review of anticoagulant exposure and access to neurocritical and neurosurgical care. The ICH protocol contains the local management and reversal instructions; also investigate the underlying vascular cause.
consider: Do examination and imaging suggest expansion or a need for escalation?
Is antithrombotic exposure verified, and has the reversal protocol been reviewed?
Is transfer or neurosurgical assessment needed, and what hemorrhage mechanism requires further imaging?
topics.caution: ICH severity scores must not be the sole basis for limiting life-sustaining treatment. A resuscitation decision does not itself limit other medical or surgical care.

sources.title: AHA/ASA 2022 spontaneous ICH guideline — official summary
sources.access: Official summary read; no drug-reversal instructions or prognostic probabilities reproduced.

topics.title: ICH: when to revisit surgical options
topics.summary: The 2026 AHA advisory updates minimally invasive surgery evidence. ENRICH found functional benefit principally in lobar ICH; MIND did not demonstrate improved 180-day function or mortality. Technique, patient selection and timing matter, so these findings are not interchangeable.
consider: How do location, volume, premorbid function and time from onset compare with the studied population?
Can an experienced surgical team assess the applicable procedure and realistic goals promptly?
Is cerebellar hemorrhage accompanied by deterioration, brainstem compression or hydrocephalus requiring urgent surgical review?
topics.caution: Technical evacuation success is not the same as proven functional benefit. Do not extrapolate selected lobar-ICH results to every deep or infratentorial hemorrhage.

sources.title: AHA 2026 minimally invasive ICH evacuation advisory — official summary
sources.access: Official summary read, including ENRICH/MIND distinctions; full advisory and surgical selection algorithm not reviewed.

sources.title: AHA/ASA 2022 spontaneous ICH guideline — official summary
sources.access: Official summary read for cerebellar hemorrhage and urgent surgical assessment; newer supratentorial MIS evidence is linked separately.

topics.title: Aneurysmal SAH: coordinated specialist care
topics.summary: Aneurysmal SAH calls for timely access to a team experienced in aneurysm treatment and neurocritical care. Priorities include securing the ruptured aneurysm, monitoring for delayed cerebral ischemia and other complications, and arranging subsequent vascular imaging and rehabilitation.
consider: Has the aneurysmal source and a plan to secure it been established with the specialist team?
Are nimodipine, volume status and surveillance for neurological deterioration being reviewed?
Could a changing examination reflect delayed cerebral ischemia, hydrocephalus or seizures?
Who owns follow-up vascular imaging and cognitive, mood and functional recovery needs?
topics.caution: This is an aneurysmal SAH reference, not a thunderclap-headache rule-out pathway. Prophylactic hypervolemia or hemodynamic augmentation is not recommended.

sources.title: AHA/ASA 2023 aneurysmal SAH guideline — official summary
sources.access: Official summary read; full guideline and diagnostic exclusion pathways were not reviewed for this card.

topics.title: Cerebral venous thrombosis
topics.summary: CVT can present with headache, visual symptoms, seizures or encephalopathy, reflecting raised intracranial pressure or parenchymal injury. CT venography or MR venography can establish the diagnosis. The AHA statement addresses anticoagulation and escalation options for severe presentations.
consider: Does the presentation and imaging warrant dedicated venous imaging?
Have pregnancy/postpartum status, hormonal exposure, infection and prothrombotic conditions been reviewed?
Are visual symptoms, seizures, consciousness changes or mass effect prompting specialist escalation?
topics.caution: Anticoagulant selection and rescue procedures depend on the clinical context. This card does not establish an individualized regimen or procedural eligibility.

sources.title: AHA 2024 CVT diagnosis and management statement — official summary
sources.access: Official summary read; full statement and treatment pathways were not reviewed for this card.

topics.title: Acute dizziness: timing, triggers and examination
topics.summary: GRACE-3 organizes acute dizziness by timing and triggers. In acute vestibular syndrome with nystagmus, HINTS is intended for trained clinicians; without nystagmus, gait assessment matters. Central or equivocal HINTS findings warrant MRI/MRA evaluation.
consider: Is this persistent acute vestibular syndrome, spontaneous episodic dizziness or triggered episodic dizziness?
Is the examiner trained, and are the syndrome and nystagmus appropriate for HINTS interpretation?
Have hearing, gait and other focal neurological findings been assessed?
Does concern for TIA in spontaneous episodic symptoms warrant vascular imaging?
topics.caution: HINTS is not a universal dizziness screen. Routine noncontrast CT is not the GRACE-3 approach to distinguish central from peripheral dizziness.

sources.title: SAEM GRACE-3 acute dizziness and vertigo — official recommendations
sources.access: Official recommendation summary read; full journal methods and evidence profiles were not reviewed. Applies to adult ED presentations with acute dizziness.

topics.title: Inpatient stroke: complication review
topics.summary: Organized stroke-unit care and systematic complication surveillance are central to recovery. Review swallowing, fever, glucose, respiratory and urinary problems alongside the neurological course. Nursing, medical and rehabilitation teams need a shared plan for prevention and escalation.
consider: Are swallowing safety and the feeding/medication route established?
Are fever, glucose, infection, urinary retention and bowel problems being addressed?
Are VTE prevention, mobility, falls and skin integrity covered by an individualized plan?
After reperfusion, are examination, access-site concerns and blood-pressure goals handed over clearly?
topics.caution: The 2026 AIS guideline advises against intensive glucose control and intensive systolic BP lowering below 140 mm Hg after IVT/EVT. Apply the treatment-specific protocol and clinical context.

sources.access: Official summary read; full statement and complication-specific recommendations were not reviewed.

topics.title: Anticoagulants: label and interaction review
topics.summary: Use the exact drug's U.S. label for the indication, formulation, renal considerations, interactions and administration requirements. AF and VTE instructions differ. Apixaban's AF adjustment incorporates age, weight and serum creatinine; edoxaban has an upper-creatinine-clearance restriction for AF. Warfarin requires individualized INR monitoring.
consider: Are the indication, current formulation, last dose, adherence and any planned procedure established?
Are current renal function, weight, age and hepatic status appropriate for the specific label?
Have P-gp/CYP interactions, other antithrombotics and nonprescription products been checked?
Do food, swallowing or feeding-tube requirements affect reliable administration?
topics.caution: A creatinine-clearance result alone does not select a dose. Review the complete current label and pharmacist input for the individual case; use the ICH protocol for urgent reversal.

topics.title: AF after ischemic stroke: anticoagulation timing
topics.summary: Timing requires an established AF indication and review of brain imaging. ELAN used imaging-defined infarct severity; OPTIMAS compared initiation within 4 days with days 7–14. CATALYST pooled initiation within 4 days versus day 5 or later.
consider: Which trial population and imaging definition fit this infarct, rather than using NIHSS as a substitute for infarct size?
Have hemorrhagic transformation, clinical stability and other contraindications been reconciled?
Is the selected drug and dose appropriate after medication, interaction and organ-function review?
topics.caution: Trial schedules do not generate an individual start date. Major infarcts and hemorrhagic transformation need their own source-specific assessment; an early-treatment result is not blanket clearance.

topics.title: Stroke mechanism, ESUS and rhythm monitoring
topics.summary: Define the mechanism before selecting prevention. For cryptogenic stroke, ACC recommends at least 14 days of rhythm monitoring when AF detection could change treatment; selected high-risk patients may start with an implanted monitor.
consider: Are arterial imaging, cardiac evaluation and relevant laboratory results complete, with competing causes assessed?
Which monitoring strategy fits the mechanism, feasibility and treatment implications?
Who will review pending results and communicate the plan?
topics.caution: A negative brief ECG does not exclude intermittent AF. Incomplete testing does not establish ESUS; empirical anticoagulation for ESUS requires a separate indication.

sources.access: Official summary checked; indexed primary guideline definition of ESUS also consulted. Full recommendation tables not re-reviewed.

sources.access: Official expert-consensus summary checked; full JACC pathway was access-restricted.

topics.title: PFO: attribution and closure discussion
topics.summary: Closure evidence is strongest for selected adults aged 18–60 with PFO-associated ischemic stroke after a competing-cause evaluation. Use PASCAL and the complete clinical assessment to support shared selection, including review of shunt and septal anatomy.
consider: Does the infarct and diagnostic evaluation support a causal PFO rather than an incidental finding?
Have alternative arterial and cardiac causes, including AF, been assessed?
Have the expected recurrence benefit, procedural complications and AF risk been discussed with the patient and closure team?
topics.caution: Neither PFO presence nor RoPE alone determines closure eligibility. Evidence beyond age 60 is limited; post-device medication and follow-up plans require the treating team's review.

sources.access: Official guideline presentation checked for patient selection, anatomy and age-related evidence gaps; full guideline not comprehensively reviewed.

sources.title: AAN PFO advisory: patient and family summary

topics.title: Carotid stenosis: symptoms, severity and referral
topics.summary: For symptomatic disease, ESO recommends endarterectomy for 70–99% stenosis and suggests it for selected 50–69% stenosis. When surgery is appropriate, benefit favors early treatment, ideally within two weeks of the last retinal or cerebral ischemic event.
consider: Are recent ipsilateral retinal or cerebral symptoms attributable to this lesion, and how was stenosis measured?
Do infarct burden, hemorrhage, disability, anatomy and procedural risk support intervention and its timing?
If asymptomatic, has the separate contemporary evidence, including CREST-2, been reviewed with intensive medical management?
topics.caution: Do not apply symptomatic thresholds or timing automatically to asymptomatic disease, near-occlusion or a large disabling infarct. CREST-2 used two parallel trials; it was not a direct stenting-versus-endarterectomy comparison.

sources.title: ESO carotid endarterectomy and stenting guideline
sources.access: Primary abstract and indexed recommendation table checked for symptomatic severity and timing; full guideline access was challenged.

sources.title: CREST-2: medical management and revascularization for asymptomatic stenosis
sources.access: Indexed primary abstract checked for asymptomatic population and parallel-trial design; no effect estimate reproduced here.

topics.title: Symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis
topics.summary: AAN's 2022 advisory prioritizes medical management: for severe 70–99% sICAS with low hemorrhagic-transformation risk, aspirin plus clopidogrel for up to 90 days; high-intensity lipid treatment; and a long-term BP target below 140/90 in clinically stable patients.
consider: Is atherosclerotic stenosis the cause of the event, with severity and territory confirmed?
Are bleeding risk, antiplatelet duration and the transition plan documented?
If events recur, have mechanism, medication adherence and specialist options been reassessed?
topics.caution: The advisory discourages stenting as initial therapy. BASIS later studied submaximal balloon angioplasty in a selected Chinese population; its findings do not establish routine acute intervention or make balloon angioplasty and stenting interchangeable. Long-term BP targets are not acute perfusion targets.

sources.title: AAN symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis advisory
sources.access: Official seven-page clinician summary read; relevant antithrombotic, stable-BP and stenting recommendations checked, not a new whole-guideline review.

sources.title: BASIS randomized trial
sources.access: Primary abstract checked for intervention, selected population, timing and procedural risks; full trial protocol not re-reviewed.

topics.title: Cervical artery dissection
topics.summary: Confirm the vascular diagnosis and distinguish cervical from intracranial or aortic disease. The AHA statement supports individualized antithrombotic selection, generally continued for at least 3–6 months, with reassessment informed by clinical and imaging findings.
consider: What do CTA, MRA or other reviewed studies show about the lesion and associated ischemia?
Which antithrombotic strategy fits the ischemic and bleeding risks, and when will it be reassessed?
Who will coordinate imaging follow-up and any targeted evaluation for an underlying arteriopathy?
topics.caution: The statement does not turn dissection into a uniform drug choice, imaging calendar or activity restriction. Recurrent neurologic symptoms require reassessment; isolated cervical dissection is not equivalent to aortic dissection.

sources.title: AHA cervical artery dissection statement: overview
sources.access: Official summary read for diagnostic modalities and individualized management.

sources.title: AHA cervical artery dissection statement: primary article
sources.access: Indexed primary abstract checked for the individualized 3–6-month antithrombotic statement; full publisher text was access-restricted.

topics.title: Secondary prevention and medication review
topics.summary: Match prevention to mechanism and review adherence. Antiplatelet plus anticoagulant treatment is usually unnecessary; DAPT has specific indications. The 2026 lipid guideline uses risk-specific LDL and non-HDL goals, with lower goals for very-high-risk ASCVD.
consider: Are antithrombotic indication, duration and planned DAPT transition explicit?
Are BP, lipid and diabetes goals individualized, with follow-up measurements and tolerance reviewed?
Do affordability, missed doses, tobacco, diet, activity or support needs require action?
topics.caution: Review the mechanism, comorbidities and current lipid-risk definition. Avoid indefinite DAPT or combination therapy without a separate reviewed indication.

sources.title: AHA/ASA secondary stroke prevention guideline: overview
sources.access: Official summary checked for mechanism-based prevention, antithrombotic limits and risk-factor care; full tables not re-reviewed.

sources.title: 2026 multisociety dyslipidemia guideline: overview
sources.access: Official summary read for contemporary risk-specific lipid goals; no complete treatment algorithm or risk classification reproduced.

topics.title: Recovery, rehabilitation and follow-up
topics.summary: The 2026 rehabilitation guideline emphasizes coordinated multidisciplinary care, repeated functional assessment and re-engagement in therapy when needs change. Screen for depression and anxiety early and again during recovery, with an evaluation and treatment pathway for identified concerns.
consider: Which impairments, daily activities and participation goals need assessment or renewed therapy?
Have the patient and care partner received appropriate education, training and support?
Is follow-up feasible, including transport, access barriers or telehealth, and who will reassess progress?
topics.caution: A screening score does not establish a diagnosis or replace clinical assessment. Recovery plans and therapy intensity need individual review; this card supplies no universal driving, work or travel clearance interval.

sources.title: 2026 AHA/ASA adult stroke rehabilitation and recovery guideline: overview
sources.access: Official summary read, published August 27, 2026; full guideline and therapy-specific recommendations not re-reviewed.

studies.title: ELAN — timing of anticoagulation after AF-associated stroke
studies.question: How did earlier DOAC initiation compare with a later schedule?
studies.population: 2,013 people with acute ischemic stroke and atrial fibrillation.
studies.comparison: Earlier: within 48 hours for minor/moderate stroke or days 6–7 for major stroke. Later: days 3–4, 6–7 or 12–14, respectively.
studies.result: The 30-day composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, major extracranial bleeding, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage or vascular death was 2.9% versus 4.1% (risk difference −1.18 percentage points; 95% CI −2.84 to 0.47). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 0.2% in both groups.
studies.limits: The confidence interval includes no difference. Trial severity categories and exclusions require review; this is not an automatic start-date rule.

sources.title: ELAN primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: OPTIMAS — early versus delayed DOAC initiation
studies.question: Was initiation within four days noninferior to starting at 7–14 days?
studies.population: 3,621 analyzed adults with AF-associated ischemic stroke at 100 UK hospitals; clinicians were uncertain about timing.
studies.comparison: DOAC initiation within four days versus days 7–14.
studies.result: At 90 days, recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, unclassifiable stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 3.3% of each group. Noninferiority met the two-percentage-point margin; superiority was not demonstrated. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 0.6% versus 0.7%.
studies.limits: Open-label treatment with masked adjudication. Apply the trial selection criteria; identical observed rates do not prove identical individual risk.

sources.title: OPTIMAS primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM. January 2025 publisher correction checked: wording and figure-at-risk count corrected; no endpoint change stated.

studies.title: CATALYST — pooled randomized evidence on DOAC timing
studies.question: What does pooled participant-level evidence show about earlier initiation?
studies.population: 5,441 participants from TIMING, ELAN, OPTIMAS and START; median NIHSS 5. Primary outcome data were available for 5,429.
studies.comparison: DOAC initiation within four days versus day five or later; individual participant data meta-analysis.
studies.result: At 30 days, recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage or unclassified stroke occurred in 2.1% versus 3.0% (OR 0.70; 95% CI 0.50–0.98). Symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage was 0.4% in each group.
studies.limits: This synthesis includes ELAN and OPTIMAS participants; it is not an independent additional randomized trial. Results retain the component trials’ selection limits.

sources.title: CATALYST primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: POINT — acute dual antiplatelet benefit and bleeding
studies.question: What was the benefit–bleeding tradeoff of adding clopidogrel?
studies.population: 4,881 patients with minor ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA at international sites.
studies.comparison: Clopidogrel plus aspirin versus aspirin alone for the 90-day trial period.
studies.result: Major ischemic events (ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction or ischemic vascular death) occurred in 5.0% versus 6.5% at 90 days (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.59–0.95). Major hemorrhage occurred in 0.9% versus 0.4% (HR 2.32; 95% CI 1.10–4.87).
studies.limits: Stopped early. Most ischemic events occurred in the first week; the 90-day design alone does not establish the optimal DAPT duration or eligibility for other stroke populations.

sources.title: POINT primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: SAMMPRIS — medical management versus intracranial stenting
studies.question: Did adding Wingspan stenting improve outcomes in severe symptomatic intracranial stenosis?
studies.population: 451 patients with recent TIA or stroke attributed to 70–99% stenosis of a major intracranial artery.
studies.comparison: Aggressive medical management plus angioplasty/Wingspan stenting versus aggressive medical management alone.
studies.result: Stroke or death by 30 days was 14.7% with stenting versus 5.8% with medical management. Estimated one-year primary-event rates were 20.0% versus 12.2%; that endpoint included early stroke/death and later qualifying-territory stroke.
studies.limits: Enrollment stopped for safety concerns. This tested a specified stent strategy; it does not directly test balloon angioplasty alone or every later device and selection strategy.

sources.title: SAMMPRIS primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract and corrected NEJM report read; source updated July 2012. Protocol and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: CLOSE — PFO closure in selected cryptogenic stroke
studies.question: Does PFO closure reduce recurrent stroke in patients with high-risk PFO features?
studies.population: 663 patients aged 16–60 with recent stroke attributed to PFO and an atrial septal aneurysm or large shunt.
studies.comparison: Closure plus antiplatelet therapy versus antiplatelets alone; the study also included a separate anticoagulation comparison.
studies.result: Over mean follow-up of 5.3 years, stroke occurred in 0/238 closure patients versus 14/235 antiplatelet-only patients (HR 0.03; 95% CI 0–0.26). Procedural complications occurred in 5.9%; AF occurred in 4.6% versus 0.9%.
studies.limits: Selected younger population with an attributed PFO mechanism. These findings do not make an incidental PFO an indication for closure or establish closure superiority to anticoagulation.

sources.title: CLOSE primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: TREAT-CAD — aspirin versus anticoagulation for dissection
studies.question: Was aspirin noninferior to a vitamin K antagonist after cervical dissection?
studies.population: 194 adults with symptomatic, MRI-confirmed cervical artery dissection within two weeks; 173 were analyzed per protocol.
studies.comparison: Aspirin versus a vitamin K antagonist for 90 days.
studies.result: The clinical/MRI composite occurred in 23% versus 15% (absolute difference 8 percentage points; 95% CI −4 to 21). Aspirin noninferiority was not established. Seven ischemic strokes occurred with aspirin and none with anticoagulation.
studies.limits: Small open-label trial; the primary composite included MRI lesions at 14 days and clinical outcomes through 90 days. Failure of noninferiority does not establish universal anticoagulant superiority; DOACs were not tested.

sources.title: TREAT-CAD primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: SELECT2 — thrombectomy in selected large-core stroke
studies.question: Does thrombectomy improve outcome in selected large-core anterior-circulation stroke?
studies.population: 352 patients with ICA/M1 occlusion within 24 hours and ASPECTS 3–5 or imaging core ≥50 mL.
studies.comparison: Thrombectomy plus medical care versus medical care alone.
studies.result: The 90-day mRS distribution favored thrombectomy (generalized OR 1.51; 95% CI 1.20–1.89). Functional independence, a secondary outcome, was 20% versus 7%.
studies.limits: Stopped early for efficacy; vascular complications occurred. Review complete selection criteria. The 2024 correction clarified core-volume measurement substitutions and stated that outcome direction and significance were unchanged.

sources.title: SELECT2 primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract and January 2024 publisher correction read; full trial report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: BAOCHE — basilar thrombectomy at 6–24 hours
studies.question: Does late-window basilar thrombectomy improve functional outcome?
studies.population: 217 analyzed patients in China with basilar-artery stroke presenting 6–24 hours after symptom onset.
studies.comparison: Thrombectomy plus medical treatment versus medical treatment alone.
studies.result: At 90 days, mRS 0–3 occurred in 46% versus 24% (adjusted rate ratio 1.81; 95% CI 1.26–2.60). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 6% versus 1%; procedural complications occurred in 11% of thrombectomy recipients.
studies.limits: Stopped at an interim analysis. The primary endpoint changed from mRS 0–4 to 0–3; the original endpoint did not show a conclusive difference. Review the trial’s full clinical/imaging selection rather than applying its time window alone.

sources.title: BAOCHE primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: DISTAL — medium and distal vessel thrombectomy
studies.question: Does EVT improve disability after selected medium/distal vessel occlusion?
studies.population: 543 participants within 24 hours; nondominant/codominant M2 or selected more distal MCA, ACA or PCA occlusions. Median NIHSS was 6.
studies.comparison: EVT plus best medical treatment versus best medical treatment alone.
studies.result: The 90-day mRS distribution did not improve significantly (common OR 0.90; 95% CI 0.67–1.22). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 5.9% versus 2.6%; mortality was 15.5% versus 14.0%.
studies.limits: A neutral trial in its selected vessel/severity population; it does not establish equivalence or settle every medium-vessel treatment question. Dominant M2 was outside the stated M2 population.

sources.title: DISTAL primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: ESCAPE-MeVO — thrombectomy benefit and safety
studies.question: Does EVT improve excellent functional outcome after medium-vessel occlusion?
studies.population: 530 patients in five countries within 12 hours of last known well, with favorable baseline imaging; most occlusions were MCA branches.
studies.comparison: EVT plus usual care versus usual care alone.
studies.result: At 90 days, mRS 0–1 occurred in 41.6% versus 43.1% (adjusted rate ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.79–1.15). Mortality was 13.3% versus 8.4% (adjusted HR 1.82; 95% CI 1.06–3.12); symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 5.4% versus 2.2%.
studies.limits: No primary-outcome benefit in this population. Vessel definition, imaging and time window matter; do not extrapolate large-vessel benefit automatically or infer a universal rule from one trial.

sources.title: ESCAPE-MeVO primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: ENRICH — early minimally invasive ICH evacuation
studies.question: Does early minimally invasive evacuation improve recovery after selected ICH?
studies.population: 300 patients with lobar or anterior basal ganglia ICH of 30–80 mL; treatment assignment within 24 hours.
studies.comparison: Minimally invasive evacuation plus guideline-based medical management versus medical management alone.
studies.result: Mean utility-weighted mRS (0–1; higher is better) at 180 days was 0.458 versus 0.374 (difference 0.084; 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.005–0.163). The benefit appeared attributable to lobar hemorrhage; 30-day mortality was 9.3% versus 18.0%.
studies.limits: Adaptive enrollment later restricted inclusion to lobar ICH. Findings concern the tested technique, timing and selected population, not all ICH surgery. Postoperative rebleeding with deterioration occurred in 3.3%.

sources.title: ENRICH primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: ANNEXA-I — hemostatic efficacy and thrombotic harm
studies.question: What were andexanet’s efficacy and safety tradeoffs in factor Xa inhibitor-associated ICH?
studies.population: 530 patients with acute ICH after factor Xa inhibitor use within 15 hours; the interim efficacy analysis included 452.
studies.comparison: Andexanet versus usual care; 85.5% of usual-care patients received PCC.
studies.result: Composite hemostatic efficacy was 67.0% versus 53.1% (adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points; 95% CI 4.6–22.2). Thrombotic events occurred in 10.3% versus 5.6%, including ischemic stroke in 6.5% versus 1.5%. No appreciable difference in 30-day mRS or mortality was reported.
studies.limits: Hemostatic efficacy is not functional benefit. This historical trial does not establish current drug availability or the preferred reversal pathway.

sources.title: ANNEXA-I primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: PRESTIGE-AF — anticoagulation after ICH with AF
studies.question: How did DOACs change ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke risk after ICH?
studies.population: 319 survivors of spontaneous ICH with AF, an anticoagulation indication and mRS ≤4; median follow-up 1.4 years.
studies.result: First ischemic stroke favored DOACs (HR 0.05; 95% CI 0.01–0.36), while recurrent ICH noninferiority was not established (HR 10.89; 90% CI 1.95–60.72). All-event rates per 100 patient-years were 0.83 versus 8.60 for ischemic stroke and 5.00 versus 0.82 for ICH.
studies.limits: The ischemic benefit and hemorrhagic harm require individualized assessment; this trial does not establish a universal restart date. Two indexed corrections could not be fully accessed.

sources.title: PRESTIGE-AF primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM. March and June 2025 corrections identified; publisher correction bodies inaccessible (403). No full corrected-report review.

studies.title: MIND — minimally invasive evacuation at up to 72 hours
studies.question: Did the Artemis evacuation strategy improve disability or survival?
studies.population: 236 adults aged 18–80 with 20–80 mL supratentorial ICH, NIHSS ≥6 and GCS 5–15; 69.5% had primarily deep hemorrhage.
studies.comparison: Minimally invasive surgery within 72 hours plus medical management versus medical management alone.
studies.result: There was no demonstrated improvement in 180-day ordinal mRS (OR 1.03; 96% CI 0.62–1.72). Thirty-day mortality was 7.2% versus 9.8% (difference −2.5 percentage points; 95% CI −11.7 to 4.8).
studies.limits: Enrollment stopped early after a feasibility analysis. Imprecision limits conclusions; do not treat the result as proof of equivalence or interchange its technique and timing with ENRICH.

sources.title: MIND primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

studies.title: SWITCH — decompression for severe deep ICH
studies.question: Does decompressive craniectomy improve outcome in severe deep ICH?
studies.population: Adults aged 18–75 with severe basal ganglia or thalamic ICH; 197 randomized participants gave delayed consent.
studies.comparison: Decompressive craniectomy plus best medical treatment versus best medical treatment alone.
studies.result: At 180 days, mRS 5–6 occurred in 44% versus 58% (adjusted risk ratio 0.77; 95% CI 0.59–1.01; p=0.057). The report characterized the evidence as weak.
studies.limits: Stopped early for funding; survival often involved severe disability. This is a decompression study in deep ICH, not evidence for every hemorrhage location or evacuation technique. Two indexed correction bodies were inaccessible.
